items.q: The bus (A) has left five minutes before we reached the station, so we (B) had to wait in the cold (C) for nearly an hour (D) without any shelter.
items.explanation: The bus left before another past event (we reached the station), so the earlier action needs the past perfect: had left.

items.q: Every one of the students (A) in our class (B) were asked to bring (C) a small plant (D) for the science fair next Friday.
items.explanation: Every one of + plural noun is a singular subject; the verb must agree with every one, not with students: was asked.

items.q: On school days my brother and I (A) usually get up at six (B) so that we can have (C) the breakfast together before (D) the earliest bus leaves.
items.explanation: Names of meals take no article when we talk about them in general: have breakfast, not have the breakfast.

items.q: The documentary (A) explains how honeybees (B) communicate with each other (C) by dancing, and it is (D) suitable to children over eight.
items.explanation: The adjective suitable is followed by for (suitable for someone), never by to.

items.q: The (A) successful of the new library depends on how many teenagers (B) are willing to walk (C) there instead of (D) staying at home.
items.explanation: After the and before of we need a noun as the subject of the sentence, so the adjective must become the noun success.

items.q: The twins (A) painted the fence (B) theirselves last weekend, although their father (C) had offered to hire (D) someone to do it.
items.explanation: The third-person plural reflexive pronoun is themselves; theirselves does not exist in standard English.

items.q: Although both lakes (A) are popular with swimmers, the water in the northern one is (B) usually (C) much more colder than (D) that in the southern one.
items.explanation: A short adjective forms its comparative with -er only; adding more as well creates a double comparative: much colder.

items.q: I (A) would certainly have bought the tickets (B) for the concert (C) last week if I (D) would have known that the band was so good.
items.explanation: In a third conditional the if-clause takes the past perfect (had known); would have belongs only in the main clause.

items.q: The guide (A) said us that the temple (B) had been built (C) more than four hundred years earlier by (D) a local king.
items.explanation: Say is not followed directly by a person; with an object we use tell: told us that (or said to us).

items.q: My aunt found (A) a box of old photographs, (B) that show the village (C) as it looked (D) before the war.
items.explanation: After a comma, in a non-defining relative clause, the pronoun must be which; that cannot introduce a non-defining clause.

items.q: Nobody in the class (A) could explain (B) why (C) had the experiment failed, so the teacher (D) repeated it the next day.
items.explanation: An indirect question keeps statement word order: subject before verb, why the experiment had failed, with no inversion.

items.q: Before the exam our teacher (A) reminded us (B) to read every question (C) carefully so that we (D) would not do careless mistakes.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is make a mistake; do a mistake is not English.

items.q: There (A) were very little volunteers at the beach clean-up (B) this morning, so the organisers (C) will hold (D) another one next weekend.
items.explanation: Volunteers is a countable plural noun, so it takes few; little is used only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: Although the rain (A) had not stopped, (B) but the marathon runners (C) set off at seven o'clock (D) as planned.
items.explanation: Although already links the two clauses; English does not add but to the main clause as well, so but must be dropped.

items.q: When I (A) got home last night, my sister (B) was cooking dinner and my parents (C) watch the news (D) in the living room.
items.explanation: Two actions in progress at a past moment (when I got home) both take the past continuous: was cooking and were watching.

items.q: The number of tourists (A) visiting the island (B) has doubled since the new ferry service (C) began, and the local shops (D) is now open every day.
items.explanation: The subject of the last clause is the plural noun shops, so it needs a plural verb: are now open.

items.q: (A) The honesty is the quality my grandfather (B) valued most, and he often said that (C) a single lie could destroy (D) years of trust.
items.explanation: An abstract noun used in a general sense takes no article: Honesty is the quality, not the honesty.

items.q: My little sister is (A) afraid (B) from spiders, so she (C) screamed when one (D) crawled across her desk.
items.explanation: The adjective afraid is always followed by of: afraid of spiders.

items.q: The chef (A) explained that the secret of his soup (B) was the (C) fresh of the herbs he (D) picked every morning.
items.explanation: After the and before of a noun is needed, so the adjective fresh must become the noun freshness.

items.q: The teacher (A) asked Minh and (B) me to hand out the worksheets, and then she (C) thanked us (D) both for ours help.
items.explanation: Before a noun we need the possessive adjective our; ours is a possessive pronoun and stands alone without a noun.

items.q: This year's (A) winter was the coldest as anyone in the village (B) could remember, and (C) the pipes in several houses (D) froze solid.
items.explanation: A superlative is followed by a relative clause with that (the coldest that anyone could remember); as belongs with as…as comparisons.

items.q: The doctor said that if my grandfather (A) had taken his medicine regularly, he (B) will not be in hospital (C) now with (D) such a high fever.
items.explanation: This is a mixed conditional (past condition, present result); the main clause needs would + base verb, not will: would not be.

items.q: When I (A) arrived at the interview, the manager (B) shook my hand and (C) asked me where did I study and (D) whether I could speak Japanese.
options: asked me where did I study
items.explanation: A reported question uses statement word order with no auxiliary did: asked me where I studied.

items.q: The village (A) where my grandparents live (B) has no supermarket, so they (C) buy vegetables from a neighbour (D) which grows them behind his house.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun refers to a person (a neighbour), so it must be who; which is used only for things and animals.

items.q: (A) Hardly I had sat down to dinner when the phone (B) rang and my boss (C) asked me to return (D) to the office.
items.explanation: When a sentence begins with the negative adverb hardly, the auxiliary comes before the subject: Hardly had I sat down.

items.q: At the end of the lesson the teacher (A) suddenly (B) said a funny joke about penguins, and (C) even the sleepiest students (D) burst out laughing.
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with joke is tell: you tell a joke, you do not say one.

items.q: The recipe needs (A) two eggs, (B) a cup of flour and (C) a few milk, but you can (D) add more sugar if you like.
items.explanation: Milk is uncountable, so it takes a little; a few goes only with countable plural nouns like eggs.

items.q: The astronauts (A) trained for two years (B) before the launch (C) so that they could cope with (D) both the noise or the shaking of the rocket.
items.explanation: Both pairs only with and (both…and); or pairs with either.

items.q: Since the new bridge (A) opens in March, the journey to the city centre (B) has taken (C) only twenty minutes (D) instead of an hour.
items.explanation: Since introduces a finished point in the past, so the verb after it is past simple: since the bridge opened, with the present perfect in the main clause.

items.q: Physics (A) is my favourite subject, but the homework (B) are often so difficult that I (C) have to ask my older cousin (D) for help.
items.explanation: Homework is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: the homework is.

items.q: The pilot (A) announced that we (B) would land in Tokyo in (C) the half an hour, (D) twenty minutes ahead of schedule.
items.explanation: The expression is half an hour; it already contains the article an, so no the is added in front of it.

items.q: The painting (A) that hangs in the hall (B) was given (C) to the school by an artist who (D) was born at this town.
items.explanation: With towns, cities and countries we use in: born in this town; at is for points or specific addresses.

items.q: (A) Unfortunate, the heavy rain (B) forced the organisers (C) to move the football match (D) to the following Sunday.
items.explanation: A sentence adverb commenting on the whole statement needs the -ly form: Unfortunately, not the adjective unfortunate.

items.q: My uncle bought a new camera (A) last month, but (B) it's lens broke when he (C) dropped it (D) on the rocks.
items.explanation: The possessive of it is its with no apostrophe; it's is short for it is or it has.

items.q: The new stadium (A) can hold twice (B) as many spectators as the old one, but the seats are (C) more narrower than (D) those we used to have.
items.explanation: Narrow forms its comparative with -er; using more as well makes a double comparative, so it should be narrower than.

items.q: Fish farms (A) would be far cleaner (B) if the owners (C) fed the fish carefully and (D) will change the water more often.
items.explanation: Both verbs belong to the second-conditional if-clause and must be past simple: fed … and changed, not will change.

items.q: The weather forecaster (A) said that it will snow in the mountains (B) that night, but (C) by morning the sky (D) was completely clear.
items.explanation: The reporting verb said is past and the forecast (that night) is already over, so will must shift back to would.

items.q: The café (A) on the corner, (B) where my parents first met there in 1998, (C) is going to close (D) at the end of the month.
options: where my parents first met there
items.explanation: The relative adverb where already stands for the place, so the adverb there inside the clause repeats it and must be removed.

items.q: Although my sister (A) has an exam (B) next week, (C) she goes never to bed before midnight, (D) which worries my mother.
items.explanation: An adverb of frequency such as never goes before a main verb: she never goes, not she goes never.

items.q: After three months at the bakery, my brother (A) no longer complains (B) about the early shifts because he (C) says he (D) is used to get up at four.
items.explanation: Be used to means be accustomed to and is followed by a noun or an -ing form: is used to getting up.
